Chapter 2: The Flaws of Monarchy and Hereditary Rule
As the colonies started questioning their ties to Britain, something big came into focus—the whole idea of monarchy. You know, rule by a single person, with power handed down through the family. For generations, kings and queens were just accepted as natural rulers. People said their authority came from tradition, or even from a higher power. But when folks stepped back and looked at their everyday lives, those old reasons suddenly seemed pretty flimsy.
Picture this: a family sitting around the fire, chatting about the latest news from England. The kids look up and ask, “Why does one family, just because of their last name, get to rule over everyone else?” The parents try to explain, maybe sharing stories about wise and just kings—but also remembering plenty of tales about rulers who were cruel, silly, or just didn’t care. It started to hit home that being born into royalty didn’t guarantee wisdom or goodness.
In the colonies, life worked differently. People respected those who worked hard and treated their neighbors right, no matter what family they came from. The idea of handing leadership down from parent to child started to feel out of place—almost backward—compared to what they saw every day.
And then, there were the practical realities. The king and his advisors were thousands of miles away, with little idea of what life was really like in America. Decisions made in London often just didn’t fit the needs of the colonies. Laws that might make sense in England could be a disaster here, where people lived among thick forests and scattered farms. The gap between ruler and ruled wasn’t just about distance—it was about understanding.
More and more, colonists started to see monarchy as not only old-fashioned, but risky. When all the power sits with one person—or one family—it’s just too easy for that power to be misused. History offered plenty of proof: wars started because of a king’s ego, laws twisted to suit a few, and harsh punishments for anyone who dared to speak their mind. Folks in the colonies had already tried self-government in their towns and assemblies—and they liked how it felt. The more they compared their own experience with the distant, unaccountable rule of a king, the more they questioned whether monarchy made any sense at all.
And what about hereditary succession? Passing power from parent to child, just because of their birth? It started to sound almost ridiculous. I mean, you wouldn’t pick a ship’s captain or a town leader just because of their family name—so why trust the future of a whole country to that system? The more people talked about it, the more monarchy looked like a relic from a darker, superstitious time—kept alive by habit and fear, not by reason or fairness.
So, in quiet fireside talks and lively public debates, a new idea started to take root: government should be based on the consent of the people, not an accident of birth. Leaders ought to be chosen for their ability to serve, not their family tree. Little by little, the colonies realized it was time to let go of the old ways—and build something better, together.
